X-70 Fractal Is the Next NASA Experimental Aircraft, Teaser Makes It Look Like a Stealth Fighter
64 photos
Photo: NASA
American space agency NASA has a very long tradition with experimental aircraft, as over the years it has used a whole bunch of them to advance both its expansion into space and the evolution of the aviation industry here on Earth. And the tradition is likely to continue, not only with its most recent X-plane, the X-59, but also with the upcoming X-70 Fractal.
The name was dropped for the first time earlier this week, during the UP.Summit at the NASA Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday. Accompanying it was a single image, a generated teaser showing the silhouette of an aircraft lost in smoke or fog, looking more like a stealth fighter jet than a benign, experimental aircraft.
The name of the plane follows NASA's established naming strategy, with X standing for experimental, 70 the number of the plane in the series, and Fractal - well, it's a mystery why this word, which usually stands for a geometric shape with a detailed structure at arbitrarily small scales, was chosen.
Described as a high-performance, highly adaptable research platform, the plane will be a piloted one, and it will be built in such a way as to have rapidly reconfigurable flight controls. This will allow the people behind the project to test things like aircraft maneuverability in ways that have never been possible before with humans inside an aircraft.
Naturally, NASA gave no further details on what that is supposed to mean, but it was mildly generous when it comes to the other capabilities of the aircraft. It shared, for instance, that it will be capable of carrying up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg) of payloads, held in a swappable fashion both inside and outside its body.
The plane's takeoff weight stands at 10,000 pounds (4,536 kg), and in flight it should be capable of reaching subsonic speeds of Mach .75 (575 mph/926 mph) and altitudes of up to 45,000 feet (13,700 meters).
NASA did not say what kind of engines will power the plane , or how many of them will be on board, but it did reveal they should be capable of taking the plane to distances of up to 1,726 miles (2.777 km) from its departure point.
The numbers above are exactly what NASA needs to accelerate the development and testing of new and innovative aviation technologies across a broad range of operating conditions. It'll be a long time, though, until it gets to do that, as the aircraft isn’t scheduled to fly for the first time until sometime in 2030.
We will keep an eye on things over the next months in the hope that NASA will reveal more about the X-70 Fractal project, including who has been tasked with making it and what will power it.
